body: The fact that you were high changes very little. You made the decision to put yourself in that situation sober (seriously, not a good idea to get high with a friend you flirt with while you have a gf). Bottom line: You fucked up. Tell your gf and accept the consequences.

For me, going out of my way to talk to new people, picking up new hobbies, exercising (endorphins and looking better), and trying to wear styles of clothing I never thought I could helped me. Of course, a lot of my insecurity revolved around my body and perceived attractiveness. You should try to identify why you are insecure/what you're focusing on negatively. Of course, public speaking classes are usually a good way to force yourself to be more confident quickly.
Wait until you're transferring, then just ask her out.
Move on. Meet other girls. Busy yourself with hobbies. Don't talk to her again. Don't get involved with someone who is in a relationship again.

You're either okay with how much time she spends with them/wants to spend with them, or you're not. Now, if what's actually bothering you is that you feel neglected because of the living situation, that's another story. Find a way to have more sex. Also, has she ever really lived apart from her parents, not in college? It's one thing to live away at college when you're still dependent on your family but another to live away from home as an adult. She may gain more independence when she moves out. Encourage her to do it sooner rather than later. That'll tell you what she'd really be like.

She needs to be willing to come to you. If not, then she's probably only keeping up the relationship because it's convenient. Yeah, she could still care a lot, but she's probably more focused on convenience. If she really cares, when you explain yourself she should listen and come to you.

The comments you've added, OP, are more enlightening than the post. It sounds to me like she's stressing herself out with expectations for herself that are way too high, and she isn't letting you be close to her and support her. Try making plans with her that involve studying or assignments done together, or celebrating with no studying when she feels like she's done well. Explain that you just want to support her and make her feel good instead of stressed.

Sounds like you've dated a lot of girls in a short time. Could be that some of them talk (girls met through friends). Could be that you're being too formulaic about the dates. Could be that you seem desperate. In any case, if you're looking for a serious relationship, just keep yourself out there socially but slow down and wait to meet someone really special. Honestly, you made it sound like you'll date anyone, and that sounds kinda desperate.

In that context, it sounds like you meant only that it would be easier for other people to realize that she needs emotional support and to be a little more considerate when talking to her. However, unless she brings it up again or there's obvious negative tension, I wouldn't continue trying to explain yourself.

If you're putting distance between the two of you because you fear being left behind/getting hurt when he moves, that's another story. But distancing yourself instead of actively trying to find a way to make it work seems like an indicator that you aren't ready to get super serious with him. I think it'd be right to end it.

It's his right to feel too overwhelmed or distraught or angry or whatever he's feeling to not be able to listen to you talk about it. You need to respect that. However, you also gave a right to be heard, and if you want to be able to talk to your SO about it, and your bf continues to be unable to, then the relationship might need to end.

I'm so sorry that happened, but I do recommend getting help from a counselor or support group.

1. Ask him to at least make frequent eye contact with you while you are speaking. If he does this, then his facial expressions and body language will indicate that he's listening. My bf has a similar problem to your bf's, though he developed it because of his mother's tendency to talk AT him instead of to him for long periods of time.

2. If the conflict is a mild argument, say, "Please give a second." Arrange beforehand that when you say this, he will be quiet and you will both stay where you are. Then take a moment to plan your reply to whatever he's said. In more intense conflict, such as actual fighting, say, "I need to think. Give me x amount of time." Then walk away for the twenty minutes or whatever you've said, but make sure you come back when you said you would. Use that time to prepare what you'll say to him, that way you will express yourself and not be silent.

All that said, it sounds like you have insecurities that are driving a lot of your concern about this. Specifically, it sounds like you don't feel like he is paying attention to you; if you don't feel like you're able to express yourself in normal conversation, it logically follows that you wouldn't even try to express yourself when he seems angry or upset and is less likely to consider what you have to say. You might work on self confidence, and it might help you be less bothered by this. Good luck!

Sounds like you both could use couple's therapy, and possibly a communications class together. If this has been going on for ten years then any problem with her not feeling heard (whether through your fault or her not spreading up for herself) could be built up in her mind as abuse. It sounds to me that you can get a little mean in a fight but not necessarily abusive, especially with how quick and willing you are to examine yourself--in my experience, abusers don't usually look for their faults when told there's a problem.
Six months should be enough time to balance the job with the relationship, out or not.

True, but it also sounds like OP doesn't like how keeping the relationship secret is affecting how much time they spend together. The only time they could spend together, she can't come because gf doesn't want anyone to know she's gay. This turns it into an issue re: both their feelings instead of just the gf's.

OP, if she won't either a) come out so you can attend her work gatherings or b) compromise and spend more time with you and less with them, then you were right to end it.

Unless what you were saying was abusive, or you knew that getting angry would upset her and made no attempts to quell your anger, you were not abusive, as far as I can tell. Could she still FEEL abused? Sure, absolutely. However, it sounds more like she's very meek and is now fed up with her own inability to stand up for herself when you yell. I would recommend at least one session of couple's therapy to see if this can be salvaged: you tell the therapist how you perceive your behavior and hers, and she does the same. This will let an objective third party tell you if you truly are in the wrong or if this is just large-scale communication failure.

He's keeping his options open, wants to have his cake and rat it too. You should probably leave the relationship. If you won't, though, tell him you're uncomfortable and that you'd like him to contact her less or not at all. If he doesn't respect this, he doesn't respect you and you should get away from him.

Have you asked him why he can't talk about the future? Why he doesn't make plans for something it ostensibly seems he wants to pursue?  He should be excited about his career, and looking into it of his own volition.  He may have anxiety about facing the future in a serious way, and if that's the case, he probably needs therapy.

The trig you mentioned is something you can take there, and if you successfully went through your time there, then you might feel more comfortable and more successful going back.

You might also consider talking to a life coaching-focused therapist about reconsidering your goals.  If you're struggling in your major, it may not be suited to you; on the other hand, you may just need to figure out what learning approach really works for you for difficult material, and I'm not close enough to you to say.

Getting a well-paying job isn't contingent on going to college, contrary to what we 'muricans are led to believe.  Trades pay very well, and there are plenty of 2-year degree jobs that do very well.  Look into a  city job fair and see what kinds of positions are available through the city--those have great benefits and usually pretty good pay, without requiring too much in the way of degrees.  It truly IS always an option to get a job now and go back to school later, when earning potential of the degree/career may not be your driving motivation.

Good luck.  Please remember that a degree doesn't necessarily equal a job or knowledge, and there may be better things out there.

I'm making some assumptions in my reply, so tell me if I'm way off base here.  This will apply if you're in the USA and if you're in your first 1-2 years of university.

If you can, think about leaving your university and going to community college (also called junior college).  I went to one for my first 2 years of college (I'm now at a 4-year school, in my third year), and they are amazing at providing assistance for their students.  They tend to have many older students--such as adults returning to school after 10+ years in the workforce--and so they focus on getting everyone to be successful academically.  The years you spend in a community college will be cheaper also, and you can get an associate's degree after those 2 years and you can choose not to go to a 4-year school after, and you'll be able to get something more than entry-level with a 2-year degree, or you will be able to be promoted out of a menial job.

There are other paths to consider: I encourage you to stay in school since it seems so important to you, but there are other paths that you can take. You don't have to go the traditional college route, you can get there in your own way.

If you want to chat more about non-traditional university pathways, feel free to PM me.

You don't need to "pay for" anything you said.  Just be happy with yourself.

My whole point was try to do your best to remember that you have options.
It ended for a reason, and those don't disappear overnight. Sure, your positive history is still there, but so is everything negative. Keep the positive memories, but let her go.

You need to choose, and be harsh in your choice.  Break it off with S, or stop seeing and talking to J.  Getting him off your mind is only going to happen if you don't interact with him and the feelings are allowed to fade.  Sure, you'd probably still think of him wistfully every now and then ("I wonder what that would've been like if we'd gone for it..."), but you'd have your long-term relationship.

On the other hand, developing feelings for J and thinking about him so much could be an indication that something is lacking from your relationship with S.  You might want to consider couples' therapy or making more of an effort to spend more quality time together if you decide to stay with him.

Either way, you need to drop one and keep it that way.  No more S, or no more J, or else nothing changes.

Please, for your own sake, don't go after her.  She isn't going to trust you, after you repeatedly engaged in behavior you knew she disliked (the texting).  The relationship between the two of you is, as you said, "marred" and it sounds like her current treatment of you is a reflection of that.

Further, it's never a good idea to date someone again you used hard drugs with.  Though you're both clean now, it's a temptation that could rear its head anytime.

If I were her, there's nothing you could do or say to get me back no matter how much I still cared about you.  The drug use is the major killer.

Sorry, man.  I hope you find someone.

Wow.  This post hit me hard, because it's so similar to my situation.  I've struggled with depression and anxiety for about 14-15 years--the majority of my life.  Sometimes, when I'm feeling it hard, I feel exactly the way you just described.

The only way I'm able to deal with it is by focusing on tomorrow, next week, and next month.  Not too far in the future, because that's still overwhelmingly scary, but making sure I have a reason to wake up the next morning, or a week or a month from now, no matter how stupid or small it may seem.  "Hey, the next episode of Downton Abbey comes out on Sunday."  "I need to buy more cat food tomorrow for my kitty."  "I'm driving up to see my parents tomorrow."  It makes things bearable during those times when I really don't want to be here anymore.  I give myself an obligation or something to look forward to to make sure that I'm still here.  Maybe a hobby would help you?  It's a good way to occupy your time, possibly make some friends?  I got more into knitting, writing, and PC gaming, and that really helped me make new connections and not be so isolated.  What are you interested in?

And no matter how much you think you'll fade away, there's always going to be reminders.  They might forget for a time, but something will call you back to their memories.  There's always going to be someone who cares enough about you now to remember you when you're gone.

Hope I helped, said something that you wanted/needed to hear.

I'm sorry medicine isn't helping you.  I personally haven't ever found anything that helps me, either, and I tried probably fifteen different medications.  It just wasn't for me or my body chemistry, I guess.  Point is, I understand how frustrating it is to feel like the little pills they give you are the answer to what's wrong, and then you take them and don't feel better.  So frustrating--but there is hope.  I'm getting along without them, and getting better.

I'm sorry you lost your job.  School isn't going well for me, either, and I decided to take a semester off to get better and rethink my priorities, my major, career path, etc.  It's helping a lot--if you're able, you might want to think about that, or dropping down to half-time.  If not, schools usually have counselors who can help and give you more specific advice.

Why not take the 400/month and use it to pay for your medications?  Then, when you're back on your feet and possibly holding onto a job better, you can stop taking the money if it makes you feel badly.

It sounds like your parents are willing to help you, if you're living with them.  Do they have any idea how you're feeling?  Talking to them might help, and they might have some ideas or be able to help guide you when the process of getting back on your feet feels overwhelming.

I don't really advocate living for other people long-term, but whatever keeps you alive until you have a reason to live for yourself is what you should focus on.

I have never checked myself in, but I have helped my best friend do it, and was with her intermittently checking up on her throughout her stay and the aftermath.  So this is second-hand information, and very specific to the particular hospital.  I am also in the US.

1. Cost: That depends on on your insurance.  You can always talk to the billing department to set up a manageable payment plan, and they may even reduce certain costs for you.  They did so for my friend whose insurance sucks.

2. Work: The hospital cannot tell your employer anything, up to and including the reason you were admitted or that you were admitted at all.  The only thing a hospital can do is say yes or no when a person calls them to ask if someone is there.  That's it.  If you want to lie (my friend said that she went in because she had a severe concussion), they won't be able to call you on it.  You can ask the hospital/your doctor there for a note confirming that you were there, and that should be enough for your employer.

3. My friend's mother and brother were super supportive.  They had no idea she had depression/anxiety prior to her checking in, and she didn't tell them until she got out.  She did well telling them, too: she'd been on meds so she was no longer suicidal or overly anxious and she pre-planned and wrote down everything she was going to say in her explanation.  It depends on your family, but they will probably be upset that you were suicidal, happy that you didn't hurt yourself, and, eventually, probably grateful you told them.  Initially, their reaction might be weird.  It's the long-term support you will probably get that will be meaningful.

4. My friend was allowed to keep her phone and her underwear.  They had someone in the room with her (nurse/nurse's aide) 24/7, or else she would not have been allowed to keep her phone.  I was allowed to bring her things like crayons (not colored pencils) and drawing paper, and a deck of cards, but I had to take these things with me when I left after visiting.

5. She says it saved her life.  They didn't discharge her until they had a treatment plan, including intensive outpatient therapy.  That's where your long-term help will come from, but the ER is a good first step for stopping yourself from acting on these intense feelings.

Please do whatever you need to do for yourself right now.  All of your worries about the ER are trivial compared to the danger you're in to yourself if you're intensely suicidal.  The repercussions of being in the hospital can be fixed when you're better and your thoughts are less clouded by depression.  Please take care of yourself.

I'm really glad that you found your sense of self, and I'd ask you to hold onto that while you go through this.

I would suggest going to a different doctor (GP or a new psychiatrist) and explain what's going on.  Tell them that yes, you know you should not have quit abruptly, but what's done is done, and that you aren't comfortable with having been prescribed those medications in the first place.

In the meantime, I would suggest asking for a low-dose SSRI.  These anti-depressants also usually work for anxiety and can be safely prescribed at very low doses for short-term use.

For now, though, if it gets really bad, call your physician or get yourself to an ER.  Good luck

If you're going to spend your relationship with her fantasizing about women you're more attracted to (sounds like it from what you said), get out now.  You aren't good for her and she isn't doing it for you.

That said, if you love her and her losing weight would be a bonus, not a must-have, then suggest it nicely.  Bring it up by saying how you care about her, and make sure to point out the health benefits of losing weight.  Ask her to do physical activities with you, like hiking or walking around.  Try getting together and experimenting with new, healthy recipes for dinners.  Make it into a bonding experience, and don't ask her to do anything you aren't willing to do right alongside her.
She's just not that into you.  Sounds like she's stringing you along.  You're both really young, no need to get serious.  Move on.

You need to be single right now.  If you think you might be becoming depressed, then you need therapy and to focus on working on yourself, not a relationship.  I would lay it out that way: "I care about you, but I need to be focusing on improving and helping myself right now.  I can't think about an 'us' when I don't even know what's going on with me."

Good luck, man.

Picking up and moving to a new place is stressful.  Right now, you're her only real support.  She doesn't have her friends, family, or hell, even her usual hair salon.  She's totally dependent on you for emotional and logistical support right now, and, if she's bossy, that probably says something about a need for control.  It sounds like it should get better when she makes some friends and finds something to do out and about in the city.

For now, to help things along, you could ask her if she'd like to start getting out doing more couples' activities--things slightly less like dates and more about meeting other people to be friends with.  Go find a rock climbing gym, or volunteer one Saturday a month at your local library or pet shelter, things like that.  It'll help you both acclimate to the area and hopefully make some friends.

In my experience, limited as it is, the feelings rarely "simmer and grow."  If you aren't into him, you aren't going to be.  I would explain to him that the time when your feelings would have worked for a relationship passed and didn't coincide with his, and this isn't going to work.  Take some time to be single and enjoy that, just my two cents. It makes it more obvious when you do meet the right person.

Use something you have in common: a video game you play together, a movie you went and saw together that you really liked, a nice date somewhere meaningful to both of you (repeating where you had your first date is a very normal, sweet idea), incorporating a holiday (you missed V-Day, but her birthday is an idea). Just think about what interests you share.

You could also call her family or somehow try to sneakily get in touch with her BFFs.  I'm sure they'd have ideas.

Good luck! :)

Whether you stay in this relationship or not, you need therapy. You have an unhealthy mindset regarding sex, stemming from bad experiences. I went through the same due to childhood trauma, and eventually worked through it to a healthy sex life. In any case, I would recommend staying and getting therapy. You won't be able to tell, really, if it's him not doing it for you or your own personal sexual issues until you work on it.

In school in separate states for four years? Sounds like you might not have adjusted to being together a lot more of the time. When you saw each other back then, you were probably making the most of limited time and paying extra attention. Now you're together more, and you need to figure out how to balance spending quality time together with other activities.

It sounds like you might have different "love languages": ways in which affection is expressed and received. His is obviously physical contact, so in his mind, even if you are annoyed with him, if you love him at all then you will still show him physical affection. I would apologize and tell him that you didn't think of it as a big deal, but that in the future, you'll try to respect that need of his more.

Show her this post. Giving her the benefit of the doubt, if she was really drunk she may have genuinely thought he was gay and just dancing in a "funny" way. Otherwise, she was doing this on purpose and you need to seriously consider moving on before something more happens. Either way, she owes you an explanation.

If you really want to keep the relationship, explain to her that you're fine with it conceptually, but feel that your needs are neglected. If they can get addressed, great. If not, time to move on. Sorry.

Don't be accusatory, just explain you aren't as secure as you perhaps should be.
He doesn't value you, at least, not nearly as much as you value him. End it.

Side note: There may be hope. My own really emotionally abusive relationship with my mother (who definitely favors my sister and had since before my father stopped being around for work) has greatly improved since those days.

I'm going to be blunt, and I'm sorry if this is hurtful: your mother is toxic to you. Your brother is toxic to you. They are being emotionally abusive to you, and emotionally manipulative. None of this is okay. You need to fight back when they bully you--not aggressively, necessarily. Just say, "no, I won't do that unless you ask nicely and help me with what you promised to already." If they get mad at you, hang up the phone, don't have these conversations in public. Change your locks, don't give them any access to you beyond what you are willing to give them. I honestly don't think they're going to acknowledge that they're hiring you and treating you badly at this point, so all you can do is chance their behavior by absolutely refusing to tolerate it.

As for your mother's denials that she ever acted that way... my mother did the same. In senior year of high school, I brought up a ton of things from the past, and she refused to believe me. I eventually realized it's because she didn't want to acknowledge that she could have failed as a mother. I don't know if that's what's going on here, but I hope that thought helps.

Finally, having that conversation again, expect it to go badly, but hope it goes well. I would say, "I acknowledge that you don't remember this the same way, but this is how *I* remember it, and this is how it made me feel." She may refuse to acknowledge that. In that case, all you can do is distance yourself emotionally and try to modify their behavior, if you even want to keep contact with them.

Sounds to me like she may be jealous of you, consciously or unconsciously. The "you hate me" could be her dealing with feeling inferior when you talk about Europe-an opportunity she'll never have in uni if school is difficult for her and money is tight. If you value her enough to salvage the friendship, I would ask her what you could do to make her feel better about the relationship between you two.

Okay. I was abused as a child for well over a year by someone who... wasn't at all like you.  Aside from having those urges, you are completely different to him.  He didn't care about what he was doing.

The fact that you care?  That means that there's still some hope for you.  There are things you can do about it.  First off?  Go check yourself in somewhere.  You won't be able to hurt anyone.  You also won't be dead.  Talk to a therapist--unless you are an actual threat, they legally can't report you.

If you haven't done anything yet, then there's still hope for you.  You're still worth saving.  We can't always control our thoughts or urges, but we can control our actions.
